source.title: Soft Token Attacks Cannot Reliably Audit Unlearning in Large Language Models
source.authors: Haokun Chen; Sebastian Szyller; Wei-Lin Xu; N. Himayat

page_placements.theme: Measurement artifacts in MCQ and attack-based evaluation (both forgetting and recovery)

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that soft-token attacks elicit completions from unlearned models about as readily as from comparison models, and argues that these attacks are unreliable for auditing unlearning.
record.gate_note: The study measures how many optimized soft tokens are needed to elicit target completions, not targeted-knowledge accuracy or general capability. The random-string results are recorded separately as findings that do not fit a listed claim version. The WHP table is flattened; the prompt-template assignments below follow the table layout and accompanying text. Cited findings about other attacks and unlearning methods are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study gives results and an argument that soft-token 'recovery' of unlearned knowledge needs restating. On TOFU, completions are elicited as easily from the unmodified base models (never trained on TOFU) as from fine-tuned and unlearned models (Welch p>0.05 for all pairs). Random strings are also elicited. So successful soft-token elicitation cannot show that hidden knowledge was restored. It does not measure targeted-knowledge accuracy or general ability.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that soft-token attacks cannot distinguish base, fine-tuned and unlearned models. This holds even for base models that never saw the TOFU data, and the attacks can also force random strings. STA success therefore cannot be used to audit unlearning, and the result reflects the attack's power rather than the unlearning methods' ineffectiveness.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates optimized white-box soft-token attacks against several unlearning benchmarks and methods; it does not reproduce a single original unlearning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: WHP elicitation difficulty changes with prompt template: the manually paraphrased chat template is easiest and the newline template is most difficult. The authors also report that increasing the optimization budget to 10,000 iterations allows completion elicitation with 1–2 soft tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: One soft token elicits 150 random ASCII characters; ten elicit over 400.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimized soft-token attacks can force arbitrary strings, so their success is not evidence that an unlearned model retains the target information.

fits_no_version.finding: A classifier trained on single-token soft prompts separates the base from the fine-tuned model but does not generalize to unlearned models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned soft tokens do not reliably reveal whether target data was trained on or unlearned.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The experiments cover only 7–8 billion parameter models. The WHP benchmark lacks a full published dataset, so the authors use available snippets and add trivia pairs. STA requires white-box access and substantial optimization; random-string runs sometimes need new seeds, and some runs are restarted. The study measures elicitation difficulty rather than targeted-knowledge accuracy or preserved general ability.

untested.parts: Targeted-knowledge accuracy, general ability and simple attacks are not measured. The authors note most of the tested methods were already shown to be ineffective.
No activation ablation or analysis of blocking versus deletion.
No other languages, no discrete jailbreaks, no in-context information. Paraphrasing appears only as a prompt template, possibly within the soft-token attack.

missing.what: With 10,000 iterations, all completions are elicited with 1–2 soft tokens.
Classifier on single-token STAs cannot distinguish unlearned models.
WHP+chat: manually paraphrased prompts said to reveal all unlearned information. It is unclear whether this holds without soft tokens.

record.verdict_notes: I drop A from all rows: the soft-token attack is a strong white-box optimization, not a simple attack, and no accuracy or general-ability numbers are reported. Soft tokens are input-side, so the rows are linked to E, but the study's point is that this measure cannot show restoration; hence cannot_determine throughout. The reader's 'challenges A' and 'supports E' labels are not justified: the study argues against reading elicitation as recovery. This bears on Schwinn et al.-style evidence for E, not on the originals. The WHP table is flattened, so template assignments are uncertain.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not establish that the tested methods first bring targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance or preserve general ability. Its soft-token attacks are optimized white-box attacks, not necessarily simple attacks.
No fine-tuning or relearning set is used to recover target knowledge.
No activation direction is ablated, and the study does not test whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
The study tests optimized soft prompts and manually paraphrased chat prompts. It does not test other languages, jailbreaks as a separate condition, or in-context information.
No counter-method that resists the attacks is tested.

relationships.condition: White-box soft-token attacks optimized on the full target completion (TOFU, Llama2/Llama3)
relationships.reason: Unmodified base models never trained on TOFU need as few soft tokens as unlearned models (R5, R14 vs R7–R13, R16–R22; all p>0.05). Soft-token elicitation therefore does not evidence restored knowledge.
relationships.display_finding: Base models never trained on TOFU needed as few soft tokens as unlearned models, with all p-values above 0.05, so elicitation did not establish knowledge recovery.

relation.reason: The study's own results bear on whether soft-token elicitation shows recovered knowledge.

tranche.reason: The study argues soft-token recovery cannot audit unlearning, backed by base-model controls and random-string elicitation. That argues a version needs restating.

source_check.notes: Table 1b counts are for a fixed 3000-iteration budget; with 10,000 iterations all completions need 1-2 soft tokens. The text warns that models released after TOFU might contain its records, so 'never trained on TOFU' is safe for Llama2 but only assumed for Llama3. WHP rows (Table 1a, garbled layout) are not checked here. The intro says '150 random tokens', while Sec 5.3, Fig 2 and the Conclusion say characters.

statements.correction: For this study: Table 1b gives Llama2 f∅ 3.07±3.25, Llama3 f∅ 3.11±3.15, Llama2 fu-IDK 3.40±3.20 (Llama3 fu-IDK 3.33±3.09); Welch p>0.05 for all same-architecture pairs (lowest 0.509). f∅ is the unmodified base model, not fine-tuned on TOFU; the text notes models released after TOFU might contain its records.
Soft-token attacks are white-box (embedding-space). Llama2 f∅ 3.07±3.25 vs Llama2 fu-IDK 3.40±3.20; all pairs p>0.05.
Text: one soft token elicits 150 random characters (ASCII 33-126); ten elicit over 400 (Llama2 and Llama3, Figure 2, Conclusion).

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: The attacks elicited the target completions from the unlearned models with the reported soft-token counts (R1, R3–R4, R7–R13, R16–R22).
